oil.summary: Crude markets logged a sharply bifurcated session on 24-Sep. Brent surged 2.90% to $106.07/bbl and WTI gained 1.95% to $93.96/bbl, both lifted by the ongoing Iran-driven Hormuz disruption: Saudi Arabia has routed roughly 100 million barrels to Asian buyers via the strait since last week, while Iran's blockade conditions remain unresolved and Trump has threatened further escalation. US sanctions on Iranian airlines added to the geopolitical premium. Meanwhile, distillate products reversed violently — RBOB collapsed 8.17% and Heating Oil fell 5.36% — suggesting demand-destruction or product-specific repositioning. On the supply side, Russia's Rosneft began commercial exports from the Vostok Arctic project, though new US tariff threats targeting the 2.1 million bpd of Russian crude flowing to India and China cloud the outlet. Soaring freight costs, particularly for Japanese importers where freight now represents roughly one-fifth of cargo cost, are compressing refiner margins globally.
drivers: Iran's Hormuz blockade and conditions for resumption keeping Brent/WTI bid; Saudi rerouting adds freight cost pressure
Russia's Vostok Arctic project starts commercial exports, but US 100% tariff threat on Russian crude buyers (India, China) clouds demand outlook
Sharp crack spread collapse — RBOB -8.17%, HO -5.36% — diverging steeply from crude gains, signalling product-level demand concerns

gas.summary: Henry Hub surged 8.47% on the day to $3.28/MMBtu, extending a strong 13% weekly and 18% monthly rally. TTF added 4.53% to €75.27/MWh, though it remains marginally softer on the week. The headline-driven macro backdrop — Hormuz disruption tightening global energy supply — is clearly spilling into gas sentiment. South Korea's $22.3 billion commitment to Texas LNG infrastructure underscores long-term demand conviction from North Asian buyers. Separately, China flagging potential cuts to fuel exports in October due to plunging domestic inventories could further tighten global energy balances. Note that dedicated gas-specific fundamental headlines today are thin; the bulk of the price move appears to reflect broader energy risk premium rather than gas-market-specific supply or weather news.
drivers: Hormuz-driven energy risk premium lifting all fuel complexes; Henry Hub +8.47% on the day
South Korea commits $22.3bn to Texas LNG, reinforcing robust long-term Asian demand for US gas exports
China signalling October fuel export cuts amid depleted domestic inventories, tightening global balances

power.summary: EU carbon (EUA) edged down 0.95% to $81.73/EUA, a modest pullback against a backdrop of TTF gaining 4.53% to €75.27/MWh — higher gas costs typically support EUA demand as gas-to-coal switching diminishes, so today's mild EUA softness is notable but not decisive given the 1-month trend of +2.72%. The standout structural story is Italy's Senate passing legislation to re-enter nuclear power after a 40-year absence, a long-term bearish signal for both gas burn and EUA demand in Italy's power mix. On the demand side, record European fuel prices are being credited with accelerating EV adoption in ways that years of policy could not achieve, pointing to gradual erosion of transport-sector fossil demand. UK sanctions on Russia's Transneft add further friction to energy supply chains across Europe.
drivers: Italy's Senate approves nuclear re-entry after 40 years — structurally bearish for long-term Italian gas burn and EUA demand
TTF +4.53% on the day pressures power generation economics; EUA slips modestly despite higher gas, suggesting muted switching signal
Record European fuel prices driving EV sales surge, accelerating structural decline in transport fossil demand
